title: Indian-American Congressman Thanedar Demands Trump Administration Halt ICE's $20 Million Shock-Glove Plan
excerpt: Rep. Shri Thanedar added his voice to growing bipartisan alarm over ICE's plan to equip officers with electric shock gloves, calling it an escalation that could lead to more abuse.
body:
• Indian-American Congressman Shri Thanedar (D-MI) called on the Trump administration to halt ICE's plan to purchase electric shock gloves for its officers.
  • ICE plans to spend up to $20 million on CTG-5 Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter (GLOVE) units, which deliver an electrical pulse on skin contact.
  • The ACLU warned that giving ICE agents "a concealed means of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability."
  • More than 50 people have died in ICE custody since Trump took office in January 2025, according to the agency's own figures.

Indian-American Congressman Shri Thanedar has called on the Trump administration to halt Immigration and Customs Enforcement's plan to equip its officers with electric shock gloves, joining a growing chorus of Democratic lawmakers and civil rights organizations sounding the alarm over what they describe as an escalation in ICE's use of force.

The Michigan Democrat's demand comes as the Department of Homeland Security moves forward with plans to spend up to $20 million on CTG-5 Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter units — or GLOVEs — wearable devices that deliver an electrical pulse on direct skin contact. DHS has described them as "Conductive Distraction and De-escalation Devices" intended for ICE deportation officers and Homeland Security investigators.

What Are the Shock Gloves?

The GLOVE units are produced by Compliant Technologies LLC, based in Lexington, Kentucky. Unlike Tasers, the gloves do not leave burn or contact marks, making it harder to document their use in excessive-force complaints. The company describes them as wearable devices rather than weapons, designed to disrupt an individual's capacity to respond.

ICE has positioned the purchase as a de-escalation tool, coming after four fatal shootings during immigration enforcement encounters since January 2025 — including two U.S. citizens shot dead by ICE agents in Minnesota earlier this year. More than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since Trump returned to office, according to the agency's own data.

Thanedar's Track Record on ICE

Thanedar, who represents Michigan's 13th Congressional District, has been one of the most vocal critics of ICE in Congress. He introduced the Abolish ICE Act in January 2026, legislation that would dismantle the agency within 90 days, and previously authored a bill to strip ICE agents of qualified immunity protections.

"They are more interested in hitting quotas and racial profiling than they are in treating people with basic respect and dignity," Thanedar said when introducing the qualified immunity bill. "No one should be above the law, especially those entrusted with enforcing it."

The congressman also led town hall protests against a proposed ICE detention center in Romulus, Michigan, a facility that ICE ultimately abandoned after a lawsuit by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel.

"Giving immigration agents a concealed means of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability."

— American Civil Liberties Union

Bipartisan Alarm

Thanedar is not alone. Senator Jacky Rosen (D-NV) called the shock-glove revelation "horrifying and infuriating," and Senator Adam Schiff (D-CA) blamed Republican lawmakers for funding ICE without constraints. New York Attorney General Letitia James warned that officers who misuse the gloves in her state could face criminal and civil consequences.

DHS defended the purchase, saying ICE officers are trained in de-escalation and that "every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards."

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

Thanedar, who was born in Belgaum, India, and immigrated to the United States for graduate school, is one of the few Indian-American members of Congress and has made immigration enforcement a centerpiece of his legislative agenda. His opposition to ICE's expanding powers resonates with Indian-American communities that have expressed concerns about racial profiling and aggressive enforcement tactics affecting legal immigrants and citizens of South Asian descent.

What's Next

The shock-glove procurement is expected to be completed by March 2027. With existing court injunctions against some ICE enforcement practices and ongoing congressional scrutiny of DHS funding, the issue is likely to remain a flashpoint through the November midterms.
